input.command:
python - <<'PYEOF'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("backend/app/services/admin_service.py")
s = p.read_text()
start = s.index("    if new_role not in WORKSPACE_ROLES:")
end = s.index("    return target\n", start) + len("    return target\n")
new = '''    if new_role not in WORKSPACE_ROLES:
        raise RoleChangeRejectedError(
            f"unknown workspace role: {new_role!r}",
            detail={"role": new_role, "allowed": list(WORKSPACE_ROLES)},
        )

    # Existence first, so a bad id is a 404 rather than a lock wait.
    if session.get(User, user_id) is None:
        raise UserNotFoundError("user not found", detail={"user_id": str(user_id)})

    # ── Everything below decides from LOCKED state, and that is load-bearing ──
    #
    # An earlier cut read `target.role` before taking the lock and gated the
    # last-admin guard on that value. Review found the bypass: with stored admins
    # {X}, actor A starts `T → viewer` while T is still `member` (capturing
    # previous='member'), stalls; B commits `T → admin`; C commits `X → member`
    # (its locked read sees {X, T}, so the guard passes); A resumes — its locked
    # read is now correctly {T}, but the guard never runs because A's *stale*
    # `previous` says T was never an admin. Result: zero stored admins. It is the
    # same read-modify-write race the lock exists to prevent, merely relocated
    # onto `target.role`, and it also made the audit line's `previous_role` a lie.
    #
    # Two locks, always in this order (target, then the admin set), so these
    # callers cannot deadlock against each other. Re-locking a row already held
    # is a no-op, which is what makes the overlap when the target IS an admin
    # harmless.
    target = session.execute(
        select(User).where(User.id == user_id).with_for_update()
    ).scalar_one_or_none()
    if target is None:  # pragma: no cover — deleted between the check and the lock
        raise UserNotFoundError("user not found", detail={"user_id": str(user_id)})
    admin_ids = set(
        session.scalars(select(User.id).where(User.role == ADMIN_ROLE).with_for_update()).all()
    )
    previous = target.role

    if previous == new_role:
        # Idempotent, and deliberately NOT an error: a UI that re-submits the
        # current value should not surface a failure. Checked BEFORE the
        # dev-bypass refusal below, so that setting that identity to the role it
        # already has stays a no-op rather than contradicting this rule. No audit
        # line either — nothing changed, and a log of non-events dilutes the ones
        # that matter.
        return target

    if target.aad_object_id == DEV_BYPASS_AAD_OID or target.email == DEV_BYPASS_EMAIL:
        raise RoleChangeRejectedError(
            "the local dev-bypass identity's role cannot be changed — it is the "
            "single operator of a dev-bypass workspace and is always an admin",
            detail={"user_id": str(user_id)},
        )

    # `target.id in admin_ids`, not `previous == ADMIN_ROLE`: both now come from
    # the same locked snapshot, but reading membership from the set that the
    # guard actually counts keeps the two from ever drifting apart again.
    if target.id in admin_ids and admin_ids <= {target.id}:
        raise RoleChangeRejectedError(
            "cannot remove the last workspace admin — promote another user to "
            "admin first. (Admins granted only by WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS do not "
            "count: that allowlist is a recovery path, not the invariant.)",
            detail={"user_id": str(user_id), "stored_admin_count": len(admin_ids)},
        )

    target.role = new_role
    session.commit()
    session.refresh(target)

    # The durable audit *table* is ADR 0020's deferred cross-entity change log
    # (#310). Until then this line is the whole guarantee that a role change is
    # never silent — so it carries actor, target, and both ends of the change,
    # and is emitted AFTER the commit so it can never claim a change that rolled
    # back. `previous` comes from the locked read, so it cannot report a value
    # that was already stale when the change was decided. Emails are omitted: ids
    # correlate, and `_PII_KEYS` redacting an `email` key is a backstop, not a
    # reason to hand one over.
    log.info(
        "workspace_role_changed",
        actor_id=str(actor.id),
        target_user_id=str(user_id),
        previous_role=previous,
        new_role=new_role,
    )
    return target
'''
s = s[:start] + new + s[end:]
p.write_text(s)
PYEOF

    the guard on it, so:

        stored admins {X}
        A: PATCH T→viewer   reads previous='member' (T is not an admin yet), stalls
        B: PATCH T→admin    commits            → admins {X, T}
        C: PATCH X→member   locked read {X,T}  → guard passes, commits → {T}
        A: resumes          locked read {T}, but the guard is skipped entirely

    This reproduces the ordering with real sessions and asserts the outcome the
    invariant promises: at least one stored admin survives. It fails against a
    guard that decides from a pre-lock read, which is exactly the shape a
    single-session test cannot express.
    """
    from sqlalchemy.orm import Session as SASession

    x_id, t_id, actor_id = uuid.uuid4(), uuid.uuid4(), uuid.uuid4()
    setup = SASession(bind=_db_engine)
    ids = (x_id, t_id, actor_id)
    try:

                User(id=t_id, aad_object_id=None, email=f"t-{t_id.hex[:8]}@e.io", role="member"),

                    aad_object_id=None,
                    email=f"a-{actor_id.hex[:8]}@e.io",
                    role="admin",

        actor = setup.get(User, actor_id)
        assert actor is not None

        s_b, s_c, s_a = (SASession(bind=_db_engine) for _ in range(3))
        try:
            # B promotes T.
            admin_service.set_user_role(s_b, t_id, new_role=ADMIN_ROLE, actor=actor)
            # C demotes X — legitimate at this point, T is now an admin.
            admin_service.set_user_role(s_c, x_id, new_role="member", actor=actor)
            # A now tries the demotion it "decided" on when T was still a member.
            # With a locked read it must be refused: T is the last stored admin.

git add -A && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
fixup: address /code-review findings on in-app role management

1. THE GUARD WAS BYPASSABLE, and the first regression test I wrote for it
   proved nothing. `previous` was captured from an unlocked `session.get`
   before the FOR UPDATE snapshot, and the guard was gated on it — so a
   stale read skipped the check entirely and could leave ZERO stored
   admins. Same read-modify-write race the lock exists for, relocated
   onto `target.role`; it also made the audit line's `previous_role`
   wrong. Now every decision comes from the locked read: the target row
   is locked first, then the admin set (one order, so these callers
   cannot deadlock), and membership is read as `target.id in admin_ids`
   rather than from a separately-captured value.

   The test matters as much as the fix. My first attempt drove the three
   sessions sequentially and passed against the buggy code too — the
   "a test that cannot express the failing case proves nothing" shape,
   caught by mutation-checking rather than by reading it. The version
   that ships exploits the fact that `session.get` answers from the
   identity map with no round trip, which makes the stale read
   deterministic instead of a timing accident. Verified to fail against
   the pre-fix code.

2. Self-demotion left `/me` stale: an admin who demoted themselves kept
   `is_workspace_admin: true`, so the Admin nav and page kept rendering
   and every later action failed with a raw 403 against a UI still
   insisting they were an admin. Refetches `/me` on a self-change —
   refetch, not a local patch, because `/me` reports the EFFECTIVE role
   and an admin still on WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS remains one.

3. `next(...)` without a default raised a bare StopIteration → a 500 with
   no error code if the row vanished between write and read, and it
   re-ran a whole-workspace two-outer-join aggregate to return one row.
   Added `get_admin_user`, sharing one row-builder with `list_all_users`
   so the two cannot disagree about what a row contains.

4. The dev-bypass refusal preceded the idempotency short-circuit, so
   setting that identity to the role it already has returned 409 —
   contradicting the no-op rule stated ten lines below. Reordered.

Both new behaviours mutation-verified. Backend 4416 passed / 97.24%;
frontend 1042 passed / 91.42% lines.

Refs #742, #744

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
